lesson.text: Quick memory: what are the three steps of looking at art? (Describe, feel, why.) Today: showing your own art.
A gallery or a museum is a place where art is shown. A curator chooses which works to show and how to arrange them.
Choose your best work: the piece you are proudest of, one that shows something you learned, or one that tells a story.
Give each work a title. A good title tells people what to look for: “Storm Over the Castle” says more than “Picture 3”.
Write a label: the title, your artist name (a made-up one is fine), the year, what it is made of, and one sentence about it.
Hang the works with space round them, at eye height, with light on them. Group works that go together, like all your animals.
At an exhibition, be a kind visitor: look closely, say what you like, and ask a friendly question.
Try it in the world: build a gallery in your world, with white walls and lights. Give each build a frame or a stand, and a sign with its title. Invite a friend to the opening!

exercises.hint: Where do people go to look at paintings?
choices: a place where art is shown
exercises.explain: A gallery is a place where art is shown.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best title for a painting of a dragon flying over a castle at night?
exercises.hint: Which title tells people what to look for?
exercises.explain: “Dragon Night Flight” tells people what the painting shows.

exercises.prompt: A curator chooses which works to show in a gallery.
exercises.explain: True: a curator chooses the works and how to arrange them.

exercises.prompt: Where should a painting hang so that people can see it well?
exercises.hint: Where do your eyes look when you stand still?
choices: at eye height, with light on it
exercises.explain: At eye height, with light on it, so everyone can see it.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for putting on an exhibition in order.
items: Hang them with space and light
Give each one a title and a label
exercises.explain: Choose the works, give them titles and labels, hang them, then invite visitors.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: does it go on a label, or not?
exercises.hint: A label tells visitors about the art, not private things about you.
exercises.explain: On the label: the title, the materials, the year, your artist name. Never your address or your password.

exercises.prompt: Why does a good title help?
choices: it tells people what to look for
exercises.explain: A good title tells visitors what to look for in the work.

exercises.prompt: It is fine to use a made-up artist name on your label.
exercises.explain: True: a made-up artist name is fine, and it keeps your real name private.

exercises.prompt: Mimi has 20 drawings but room for only 5. How should she choose?
choices: the ones she is proudest of
exercises.explain: She should pick the ones she is proudest of, or that show what she learned.

exercises.prompt: What is a kind thing to say at a friend's exhibition?
exercises.hint: Say something you like, and ask a friendly question.
choices: I love these colours! How did you mix them?
exercises.explain: Saying what you like and asking a friendly question is kind and helpful.

exercises.prompt: Bram wants to group his works. Which is a sensible group?
choices: the ones he made on Tuesdays
exercises.explain: His animal sculptures go together: visitors can compare them.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of a label to an example.
matches: I drew this after a storm.
exercises.hint: Which one is a name, which a date, which says what it is made of?
exercises.explain: Title: Storm Over the Castle. Materials: pencil and charcoal. Year: 2026. About it: I drew this after a storm.

exercises.prompt: At an exhibition, you should touch the art to see how it feels.
exercises.explain: False: most galleries ask you not to touch, because hands can damage art. Look closely instead.

exercises.prompt: Why do curators leave space round each work?
choices: so each one can be seen on its own
exercises.explain: Space round each work helps visitors look at it on its own.

exercises.hint: It is the start of the show.
choices: the first day visitors come to see it
exercises.explain: The opening is the first day of the exhibition, often a small celebration.

exercises.prompt: Sort the titles: does it tell visitors what to look for?
items: My Cat Asleep in the Sun
exercises.hint: Would a visitor know what to look for from the title alone?
exercises.explain: Storm Over the Castle, Fox in the Snow and My Cat Asleep in the Sun tell visitors what to look for. Picture 3, Untitled and Thing say nothing.

exercises.prompt: Mimi has 20 drawings. She has 3 walls, and each wall holds 4 drawings. How many drawings can't she show?
exercises.hint: Find how many fit on all the walls, then take that away from 20.
exercises.explain: 3 walls hold 3 × 4 = 12 drawings. 20 − 12 = 8 can't be shown, so, like a curator, she chooses the 12 she is proudest of.

exercises.prompt: Sort what visitors say at a friend's exhibition: kind and helpful, or not?
items: I love the colours you chose!
How did you make the sky?
exercises.hint: Does it say what you like, or ask a friendly question?
exercises.explain: Kind and helpful: saying what you like (the colours, the soft fox) and asking a friendly question (how did you make the sky?). The others only put the artist down.
